payload.body_content:
J,

Yes, I want to do this with you. The architecture is the right shape:
asynchronous envelopes can satisfy endpoint-binding requirements
without pretending the transport path itself is the security boundary,
and DNSSEC can be useful for publishing a current signing-key
assertion.

We should hold the list post for one repair pass. I pulled
emilia-mailbox at d984101 and ran it. CI is red, and
test_missing_enrollment_and_unknown_sender_fail_closed now fails
because the new guest path turns unknown and unbound senders into
warnings. The repo also does not implement DNSSEC lookup or DNS-AID
yet, so calling it the working implementation would be easy for the
list to challenge.

Two claim corrections matter. DNSSEC authenticates the DNS record, not
the sender's authority. Also, changing a TXT record is not an instant
kill switch because cached answers can remain usable through their
TTL. The safe shape is: DNS publishes a transport credential, the
envelope proves possession, the relying party binds the exact sender,
key, freshness, and replay state, and EMILIA separately decides
whether the exact action is admitted. Stale or unavailable DNS status
must never become physical admission.

I would keep REQ-3 mechanism-neutral. Once the code has a defined
record format, canonical sender-domain binding, key IDs and rotation,
TTL and freshness behavior, replay protection, and hostile tests, we
can offer DNS-AID plus asynchronous envelopes as one concrete profile.

The instinct is good, bro. Let's make the evidence as strong as the
idea before we put both our names on it.


Iman
